content.summary_of_the_paper: Following works like Maretic. et.al., a graph is represented as a Gaussian random variable. Sinkhorn divergence between the Gaussians representing two Graphs is defined as the distance between the graphs. This also provides a map/alignment between the graphs. This computation can be done analytically using works like Feydy et al. (2019); Mallasto et al. (2021). The proposed methodology is compared to works like Maretic et.al., on graph alignment, sketching and retrieval.

content.summary_of_the_paper: In this paper, the authors consider the entropy-regularized optimal transport between graphs and derive the close-form expression under the properties of Gaussian geometry. They further propose to consider the 2-Sinkhorn divergence to control the bias. Numerical experiments show that the proposed approach works better than existing methods on the task of graph alignment, graph sketching, and graph retrieval in some data sets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. The close-form expression of the optimization objective on Gaussian geometry makes the whole problem to be solvable.
2. Lots of experiments demonstrate the strength of the proposed framework in these graph-based tasks.

Weakness:
1. Entropy-regularized OT has emerged as a solution to the computational issue of OT and has been widely considered in the literature. Since the only difference between the approach in this paper and the existing methods is entropy regularization (2-Sinkhorn divergence has been studied in other papers to control the bias), I seriously double the novelty of this paper.
2. The authors claim the theoretically faster convergence of their approach to empirically higher performance. However, I do not find any theorem to support this argument. It would be great if there is any theoretical analysis to demonstrate the strength of the proposed framework except for experiments.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: This paper is well-organized and easy to follow. Both the quality and clarity are good. My main concern is its novelty. Given that entropy-regularized OT has been well-studied in the literature, I am afraid the originality is quite rare.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper mainly derives the close-form expression of entropy-regularized optimal transport and applies the SGD to solve it. Numerical results demonstrate its strength. However, since entropy-regularized OT has been well-studied in the literature, I believe the contribution of this paper is limited, so I recommend rejecting this paper.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors consider the optimal transport problem for graph comparison. The authors extend the Graph Optimal Transport (GOT) by following the graph-signal representation for graph (i.e., as a Gaussian) and propose to use either entropic-regularized OT (i.e., Sinkhorn) or Sinkhorn divergence instead of the standard OT as in GOT. Inheriting properties from Sinkhorn/Sinkhorn divergence for Gaussian distributions, the proposed method (ErGOT) has a low sample complexity, interpolation between OT and MMD, unbiased property, closed-form for computation.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
(*) Strength:
+ The authors extend GOT by replacing standard OT by either entropic regularization OT or Sinkhorn divergences for Gaussian representation for graphs to inherit several nice properties.
+ The proposed ErGOT performs well in applications.

(*) Weaknesses:
+ The novelty seems modest since it is a direct extension of GOT incremental (using the same graph-signal to represent a graph as Gaussian distribution and replacing standard OT by Sinkhorn/SInkhorn divergence). 
+ The properties of the proposed ErGOT directly inherit from Sinkhorn/Sinkhorn divergence for Gaussian distributions in the literature.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
It is easy to follow the flows of the submission. The proposed methods (ErGOT) performs well in applications.
However, as mentioned in the strength and weaknesses, ErGOT seems a direct extension of GOT by using the same graph-signal to representation graph as a Gaussian distributions and replacing standard OT by either entropic regularized OT or Sinkhorn divergence. The derived properties of ErGOT are not surprising by directly inherited from Sinkhorn/Sinkhorn divergence for Gaussian distributions.

Some concerns are as follows:
+ For problem (5), could the authors elaborate more about motivation of using the parameterization for Gaussian variance by the permutation matrix M (even though it follows from GOT approach).
+ For two graphs with different number of nodes, is the problem (5) still applicable (as in the COPT by Dong & Sawin'2020)? 
+ The problem (5) is non-convex, how does one choose the initialization (and how the initialization affects the algorithm)?
+ Why ErGOT is faster than GOT? (it seems that the closed-form of ErGOT is even more complicated than GOT, recall that ErGOT uses Sinkhorn/Sinkhorn divergence while GOT uses the standard OT over graphs represented by Gaussian distributions. It is better if the authors elaborate this observation with more details
+ Do \tau and \epsilon affect the performances of ErGOT? It is better if the authors elaborate why the authors can fix value for \tau and \epsilon for ErGOT in experiments?
content.summary_of_the_review: The proposed method obtains good performances in applications. It seems that the novelty is modest.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors propose an entropy regularized version of optimal transport between graphs with a framework called ErGOT, and apply it to tasks on alignment, sketching and retrieval. The core proposal is to add a KL entropy regularization term to the optimal transport objective, and to control the bias using a Sinkhorn divergence approach.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
- Strengths: 

The proposed framework is natural, the problem that they are tackling is of interest/importance. 

The experimental/empirical evaluations are quite comprehensive and shows generally good performance for sketching tasks and ok performance for retrieval tasks. 

- Weaknesses: 

Exposition: The writing is not very clear and well exposed. Starting from section 3, while they motivated the use of Gaussians to represent graphs nicely and well, starting with the classic GOT approach section, the authors rapidly introduced multiple objectives and expressions with minimal motivation, only deferring to references/the appendix for details. I think this makes the paper hard to follow for a general audience. I suggest expanding the introduction in this section to improve the exposition. 

Approach: Their approach is to basically add a KL term as regularization to the optimization problem. While this approach is certainly very natural and novel to the best of my knowledge, I am not satisfied with the originality or extent of their theoretical justification. Basically, most of the authors theoretical justifications/derivations of closed form expressions are very direct extensions/applications of results from other papers (e.g. expressions 5, 6, 7, 10). 

The technically more original thing that they did is the bias control framework, where they used a Sinkhorn divergence that interpolates between OT and MMD. I find this unsurprising. With any penalization, there is associated shrinkage, so of course when one adjust the tuning parameter it interpolates between two objectives. This is the property of many shrinkage/penalty/Bayesian estimator. 

To improve the technical aspect of the paper, I think the authors need more original results that go beyond their current results. 

- Minor Issues: 

Much of the citation formatting is off (parenthesis missing when citing papers...perhaps use \citep instead). 

- Missing references: 

The following references are relevant papers in graph comparison (without alignment information, some using optimal transport): 

Network Portrait Divergence: An information-theoretic, all-scales approach to comparing networks. James Bagrow and Erik Bollt

Embedded Laplacian Distance: Multiscale Graph Comparison via the Embedded Laplacian Distance. Edric Tam, David Dunson

Graph Diffusion Wasserstein Distance: Barbe et. al. Graph Diffusion Wasserstein Distances. ECML-PKDD 2020
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is written only in a moderately clear way. I have provided suggestions for improvement. 

The quality of the experimental evaluation is good, however, the quality and originality of the technical/theoretical contributions is in my opinion lacking.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, it is a natural idea that the authors are proposing, and the evaluations experimentally are decent. The main issue is their lack of technical depth/theoretical analysis that hampers the quality of this paper. If the authors could provided more in depth theoretical claims, this has the potential to become a good paper.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
